source.title: Open Problems in Efficient Semi-Supervised PAC Learning

accepted.question_text: Let C be a concept class, let χ be a compatibility notion for unlabeled data, and let D be a data distribution. For ε > 0, define C_{D,χ}(ε) = {h ∈ C : 1 − χ(h, D) ≤ ε}. Assuming the target hypothesis belongs to C and is fully compatible with D, unlabeled data can in principle shrink the search space from C to C_{D,χ}(ε), so that information-theoretically one would hope to learn using on the order of (1/ε)(log |C_{D,χ}(ε)| + log(1/δ)) labeled examples, or a quantity polynomial in this bound. The open question is whether, for interesting choices of C and χ, there exist computationally efficient semi-supervised learning algorithms that achieve labeled-sample complexity matching this bound up to polynomial factors.

evidence.quote: For a given class C, compatibility notion χ, and distribution D, define CD,χ(ε) = {h ∈ C : 1 − χ(h, D) ≤ ε}. Under the assumption that the target belongs to C and is fully compatible, then given enough unlabeled data we can in principle reduce our search space from C down to CD,χ(ε). Thus, we should in principle need at most O(1/ε (log |CD,χ(ε)| + log 1/δ)) labeled examples to learn well.
The high-level question is whether for interesting classes C and notions of compatibility χ, one can learn with this many (or polynomial in this many) labeled examples by efficient algorithms.

accepted.question_text: Consider the semi-supervised PAC model for the class C of two-sided disjunctions over {0,1}^n. A hypothesis h is a pair of disjunctions (h+, h−), where only h+ is used for classification, and h is deemed compatible with the distribution D exactly when, for every example x, h+(x) = −h−(x), so the positive and negative classes are both representable by OR-functions. The open question is whether there is a computationally efficient semi-supervised learning algorithm for this class and compatibility notion that uses as few labeled examples as the compatibility-filtered search space suggests, up to polynomial factors.

evidence.quote: Two-sided disjunctions: This is a generalization of the example above where we now allow variables to be positive indicators, negative indicators, or irrelevant. Specifically, define a “two-sided disjunction” h to be a pair of disjunctions (h+, h−) where only h+ is used for classification, but h is compatible with D iff for all examples x, h+(x) = −h−(x). That is, D is such that both the positive and negative classes can be described by OR-functions.
We now instantiate this high-level question with a few specific classes and compatibility notions.

accepted.question_text: Suppose every variable is either a positive indicator or a negative indicator, and replace the strict compatibility condition from the monotone-disjunction example with a margin-style requirement: a positive example must contain at least 60% of the positive indicators and at most 40% of the negative indicators, while a negative example must satisfy the analogous reversed condition. The open question is whether this two-sided-majority-with-margins setting admits a computationally efficient semi-supervised PAC learning algorithm with labeled-sample complexity matching the small compatible-search-space intuition up to polynomial factors.

evidence.quote: Two-sided majority with margins: As a different generalization of the problem from Section 3.1, suppose that again every variable is either a positive or negative indicator, but we relax the margin condition a bit. In particular, say we require that x either contain at least 60% of the positive indicators and at most 40% of the negative indicators (for positive examples) or vice versa (for negative examples).
The high-level question is whether for interesting classes C and notions of compatibility χ, one can learn with this many (or polynomial in this many) labeled examples by efficient algorithms.

accepted.question_text: Consider co-training in which the hypothesis class C is the class of disjunctions, each unlabeled example is a pair (x1, x2) of points in {0,1}^n, the classifier predicts using h(x1), and compatibility requires h(x1) = h(x2). Equivalently, each unlabeled pair is assumed to consist either of two positive examples or of two negative examples. The open question is whether there is a computationally efficient semi-supervised PAC learning algorithm for this co-training-with-disjunctions model that achieves labeled complexity close to the compatibility-based information-theoretic bound.

evidence.quote: Co-training with disjunctions: This is the “inverse” of the two-sided disjunction problem. Let C be the class of disjunctions, but an example x is a pair of points (x1, x2) in {0, 1}^n. Define h(x) = h(x1) but say that h is compatible with x iff h(x1) = h(x2). That is, under our compatibility assumption, each unlabeled example is either a pair of positive examples or a pair of negative examples. Note that D is now a distribution over pairs.
The high-level question is whether for interesting classes C and notions of compatibility χ, one can learn with this many (or polynomial in this many) labeled examples by efficient algorithms.

accepted.question_text: Consider the co-training setting in which the hypothesis h is a linear separator and each unlabeled example is a pair (x1, x2). Efficient algorithms are known in the special case where x1 and x2 are drawn independently conditional on their label, but the general consistency problem is NP-hard. The open question is whether one can relax the independence-given-the-label assumption in a nontrivial way and still obtain a computationally efficient algorithm for this class.

evidence.quote: Co-training with linear separators: A generalization of the above problem is the case that h is a linear separator. It is known that the consistency problem is NP-hard [A. Flaxman, personal communication], however efficient algorithms are known for the special case that the elements x1 and x2 of the pair are drawn independently given their label [3, 1]. Even if one cannot solve the problem efficiently in general, a natural question is whether one can at least weaken the independence-given-the-label assumption in a nontrivial way and still get an efficient algorithm for this class.

accepted.question_text: Beyond the concrete cases listed in the note, the broader open problem is to identify additional concept classes C and compatibility notions χ in the semi-supervised PAC model for which unlabeled data can be exploited by computationally efficient algorithms to reduce labeled sample complexity in the sense suggested by the compatibility-filtered search space.

evidence.quote: More generally, it would be interesting to consider other classes and notions of compatibility as well.
The high-level question is whether for interesting classes C and notions of compatibility χ, one can learn with this many (or polynomial in this many) labeled examples by efficient algorithms.
